Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

vignette:
Mai, a 51-year-old dentist in a small suburban practice, still remembers the precise hum of the song that used to play from her stalker’s phone. It had been five years since the former patient—a quiet man she’d treated for a routine filling—began leaving notes on her car windshield, then waiting outside her clinic, then following her home in evenings. She called the police twice, but he always disappeared before they arrived, and without a direct threat they could only file a report. One night he stood beneath her bedroom window, the song looping softly through the dark. That was the night something shifted permanently inside Mai. She finally obtained a restraining order after he left a voicemail whispering the lyrics, but by then the damage was done. Even after his arrest and a brief jail sentence, Mai could never shake the certainty that she was still being watched.

In the months that followed, the world itself became a map of hazards. A familiar melody from a passing car, a television report about another stalking case, even the sight of a police cruiser—each triggered an immediate and visceral flooding of dread. What frightened Mai most was that these moments did not pass. They left a residue: she would find herself scanning every room for exits, choosing a seat only if it offered a clear view of the door and a wall at her back. She came to believe that safety was an illusion, even when her husband reassured her that the man was gone. “They say he’s in another state,” she would whisper, “but they said that before.”

Every day at her dental practice, Mai enacted these rules unconsciously. She positioned her office chair so her back faced the corner, her eyes trained on the hallway. When the receptionist played soft pop in the waiting area and an old song from that period came on, Mai excused herself to the break room until it finished. She avoided all true-crime media, but even a brief newspaper headline about harassment could leave her jittery for the rest of the afternoon. And police—the very people who initially could not prevent the stalker—made her feel paradoxically more exposed; seeing a squad car parked near the clinic would bring back the image of the officer shrugging, saying there wasn’t enough evidence.

These triggers did not merely remind Mai of the past; they actively eroded her capacity to feel safe in the present. She began arriving home only after dark, always checking her rearview mirror, and she insisted that they sit in the corner booth at restaurants, her back solid against the wall. Her husband grew frustrated—he wanted to go to concerts, to parties, to simply walk the block—but Mai could not explain why her body refused to believe any reassurance. What she felt was not a memory; it was a living threat that flickered back to life whenever the wrong sound or image appeared.

Mai finally sought help because her husband, with gentle desperation, told her he could not watch her shrink away from life any longer. She came to the first session with her hands clasped tight, unable to fully commit to the idea that talking could help. “I know he’s gone,” she said, her voice barely above a whisper, “but something inside me still believes he’s out there, ready to start that song again.” What she hoped—what she was afraid to hope for—was that she might one day walk into a room without first plotting her escape.
